title: Browse Mode, Focus Mode, and the Rotor: How NVDA and VoiceOver Actually Move
description: NVDA's browse/focus split and VoiceOver's Quick Nav and Rotor are two different navigation models for the same job — knowing which one is active is the difference between reading a page and being stuck inside a widget on Havenmark's product listing.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish NVDA browse mode from focus mode and identify which is active from the announcement alone
Use VoiceOver's Rotor and Quick Nav to survey a page's structure the way NVDA's Elements List does

contentSections.body: You're auditing Havenmark's product listing page — the one with 40 sofas, a filter sidebar, and a sort dropdown. You land on it in NVDA and press `H` to jump through the headings. Nothing happens. You try `Tab`. Also nothing. The page hasn't crashed — NVDA is in focus mode, because the page loaded with keyboard focus already sitting inside the filter sidebar's custom multi-select widget, and NVDA auto-switched into focus mode the moment it detected an editable or app-like control. Every keystroke you're sending is going straight to that widget, not to NVDA's page-reading commands. A developer testing this with a mouse would never see it. You only found it because you were listening to which mode NVDA said it was in — and you weren't, yet, which is exactly why `H` didn't work.

**Try it before you read on.** Open NVDA on a real page with a form on it — any newsletter signup will do. Tab into the email field and listen: NVDA announces something like "edit, blank" and the pitch changes slightly. Now press `NVDA+Space`. Listen again. That's the toggle you'll be reasoning about below.

NVDA and VoiceOver solve the same problem — let someone read a page's structure *and* operate its controls with the same keyboard — with genuinely different models. Confusing the two is the single most common way an accessibility QA engineer misreads a screen reader session.

**NVDA: browse mode and focus mode are separate, and NVDA switches between them for you.** Browse mode is the default for reading content — NVDA builds a virtual buffer of the page and lets you move through it with single letter keys: `H` for headings, `D` for landmarks/regions, `T` for tables, `F` for form fields, `B` for buttons, arrow keys to read line by line. Focus mode hands every keystroke straight to the page — this is what you need inside a text field, a `<select>`, or a custom widget like a date picker, because in focus mode `H` types the letter "h" instead of jumping to a heading. NVDA switches to focus mode automatically when you tab into most form controls, and switches back to browse mode when you tab out — but it can get this wrong on custom widgets that don't expose the right role, which is exactly what happened in the hook. `NVDA+Space` forces a manual switch either direction, and is the first thing to try when your navigation keys stop working.

**VoiceOver doesn't have a browse/focus split — it has Quick Nav and "interacting with."** Quick Nav (toggled by pressing Left Arrow and Right Arrow together) lets the arrow keys alone move you item by item through the page — headings, links, and controls all in one linear sequence, activated with `VO+Space` (`VO` is Control+Option by default). Where VoiceOver diverges from NVDA is complex or grouped content: a table, a custom listbox, a widget VoiceOver has bundled into one stop. You have to explicitly *interact with* it — `VO+Shift+Down Arrow` — before arrow keys will move between its internal parts, and `VO+Shift+Up Arrow` to back out again. Forgetting you're "interacting with" a group is VoiceOver's version of NVDA's stuck-in-focus-mode problem: your arrow keys are moving inside the widget, and you don't know why the rest of the page isn't reachable.

contentSections.scenario: Havenmark's product listing. You tab onto the page and NVDA says: "Sort by, combo box, Price low to high." You press `H` to jump to the next heading. NVDA reads back: "h" — as in, it typed the letter into something.
contentSections.question: What does this tell you about NVDA's current mode, and what's the fix?

options.label: NVDA is in focus mode because it's parked on a combo box — press NVDA+Space, or Escape out of the widget, to get back into browse mode before trying heading navigation
NVDA has stopped responding to commands and needs to be restarted
The page genuinely has no headings, and NVDA is reporting that the only way it can

feedback.focus-mode-active: Correct. Landing on a `<select>`-style combo box is one of the standard triggers for NVDA's automatic switch into focus mode, because a combo box needs its own arrow-key behaviour (moving between options) that would conflict with browse mode's letter-key reading commands. `H` got typed as a literal character because, in focus mode, that's what a printable key does. NVDA+Space toggles back to browse mode, or pressing Escape backs out of the combo box entirely and NVDA reverts on its own.
feedback.nvda-broken: NVDA is working exactly as designed here — this is a mode issue, not a crash. Restarting would just land you back in the same combo box, in the same mode, with the same result.
feedback.page-has-no-headings: NVDA reporting a typed "h" is a specific, recognizable signal of focus mode, not of an empty heading list. If there were genuinely no headings, `H` in browse mode would announce "no next heading" — a completely different message from a letter being typed into a field.

contentSections.mechanism: NVDA infers which mode you need from what has focus, not from what you're trying to do — a combo box, listbox, or text field puts it in focus mode by default because those widgets need to receive raw keystrokes for their own interaction model to work. The mode is silently attached to the control, which means the two most useful diagnostic habits are: listen for what NVDA calls a control when you land on it ("edit," "combo box," and "list box" all typically mean focus mode is coming), and if a browse-mode command produces an unexpected result — like a letter appearing somewhere — check the mode before assuming the page is broken.

contentSections.scenario: You're building a mental model of when NVDA switches into focus mode on its own, versus when you have to force it with NVDA+Space. Sort the following.
contentSections.question: Select every situation where NVDA switches to focus mode automatically, without you pressing NVDA+Space.

items.label: Tabbing into a text input
Tabbing into a native <select> dropdown
Landing on an element with role="application"
Pressing H to move to the next heading on a content-only page
Arrowing down through body paragraphs in browse mode
Tabbing onto a plain text link with no ARIA role overrides

explanation.tab-into-textbox: Switches automatically. A text field needs to receive the letters you actually type, so NVDA hands keystrokes straight through the moment you land on one.
explanation.tab-into-native-select: Switches automatically. Native selects use arrow keys to move between options — the same keys browse mode uses to read line by line — so NVDA resolves the conflict by switching modes for you.
explanation.aria-application-role: Switches automatically. role="application" is a page author's explicit signal that this region manages its own keyboard interaction (a rich widget like a spreadsheet or code editor), so NVDA gets out of the way for all of it. It's also the role most likely to be applied wrongly — on ordinary content it strips away every browse-mode command a user relies on for no benefit.
explanation.heading-navigation: Stays in browse mode — this is what browse mode is for. If H stops working here, something is wrong, not something that switched deliberately.
explanation.reading-a-paragraph: Stays in browse mode. Reading content with arrow keys is the default, uninterrupted case.
explanation.landing-on-a-plain-link: Stays in browse mode. A link activates with Enter but doesn't need its own keystrokes the way a combo box does, so there's no conflict to resolve.

contentSections.synthesis: The pattern: NVDA switches to focus mode for anything that needs to consume the same keys browse mode uses to navigate — text entry, arrow-key-driven widgets, and anything explicitly marked as managing its own interaction. Everything else stays in browse mode. When you find yourself on a custom widget and the mode didn't switch when it should have, that's usually a missing or wrong ARIA role — the same category of bug as the sidebar in this lesson's hook.

contentSections.scenario: Same product listing page, now open in Safari with VoiceOver. You land on the filter sidebar, which is built as a set of custom checkboxes inside a `<div role="group">`. VoiceOver announces the group and its label, then goes quiet when you press the Right Arrow.
contentSections.question: What's the most likely reason arrowing further does nothing?

options.label: VoiceOver is treating the group as one stop and hasn't been told to interact with its contents yet
VoiceOver has stopped tracking keyboard input
The group genuinely has no focusable content inside it

feedback.not-interacting: Correct. VoiceOver treats a grouped or complex region as a single navigation stop by default — you have to explicitly interact with it, via VO+Shift+Down Arrow, before Right Arrow will move you between the checkboxes inside. Until then, VO thinks it's already given you everything that stop has to offer, so arrowing again moves past the whole group rather than into it.
feedback.voiceover-crashed: A silent Right Arrow press is the expected, working behaviour of a grouped stop VoiceOver hasn't been told to enter — not a sign anything has failed.
feedback.group-is-empty: The checkboxes are there — you heard the group get announced with a label, which means VoiceOver found content worth grouping. The content isn't reachable yet, which is a different problem than it not existing.

contentSections.concept: VoiceOver's "interacting with" state is the direct counterpart to NVDA's focus mode, but the trigger is different: NVDA switches based on what kind of control has focus, while VoiceOver switches based on an explicit command you give when you land on something it has grouped. Both failure modes look identical from the outside — keys that should move you somewhere are doing nothing — and both have the same first diagnostic step: name out loud what VoiceOver or NVDA just announced, because the announcement tells you which state you're in before you touch another key.

contentSections.body:
One more tool belongs in this lesson, because it replaces guesswork with a direct survey of the page: NVDA's **Elements List** (`Insert+F7`) opens a dialog with tabs for Headings, Landmarks, Links, Form Fields, and Buttons, each filterable by typing. It's the fastest way to answer "does this page even have headings" before you spend three minutes arrowing through content trying to find out. VoiceOver's equivalent is the **Rotor** (`VO+U`): Left and Right Arrow switch between categories — Headings, Links, Form Controls, Landmarks, Tables — and Up/Down Arrow moves within the selected category, with Return jumping you straight to that item on the page.

Both are survey tools, not reading tools — open one at the start of an audit to build a map of the page's structure before you commit to tabbing or arrowing through it line by line. On Havenmark's listing page, opening the Elements List's Headings tab first would have told you in two seconds whether the product grid uses one `<h2>` per product (accessible, if verbose) or none at all (a genuine structure gap) — instead of discovering it by trial and error while also fighting the focus-mode problem from the hook.

contentSections.question: You've just opened Havenmark's product listing page for the first time in NVDA. Put these steps in the order that actually builds an accurate picture of the page, rather than a confused one.
steps: Confirm you're in browse mode before doing anything else
Open the Elements List (Insert+F7) and check the Headings and Landmarks tabs
Close the Elements List and Say All (Insert+Down Arrow) through the page once
Tab through interactive controls individually, noting any unexpected mode switch
Write down which controls put NVDA into focus mode and whether that matches what the control actually is
contentSections.explanation: Checking the mode first matters because every command after it is meaningless if you're not in the mode you think you're in — the hook in this lesson is exactly what happens when you skip this. The Elements List comes before Say All because it gives you the page's skeleton fast, so the read-through that follows has a map instead of being a blind first pass. Tabbing through controls individually comes after the overview, not before, because now you're checking something specific — whether each control's mode switch matches its actual role — rather than discovering structure by accident. Writing down the focus-mode mismatches last turns a testing session into a finding: a custom multi-select that never triggers focus mode, or a plain link that inexplicably does, is a concrete defect with a concrete location, not a vague impression you'll have forgotten by the time you write the report.

contentSections.body: NVDA has two modes and switches between them based on what has focus; VoiceOver has one linear model plus an explicit "interact with" step for grouped content. Neither difference is trivia — it's the first thing to check whenever a navigation key stops doing what you expect, before you conclude the page itself is broken.

title: Headings, Landmarks, and Tables: Structure a Screen Reader User Actually Relies On
description: A heading that's the right level but the wrong words, a landmark that exists but isn't labelled, and a comparison table that reads as a wall of numbers — three ways structural markup passes a scan and still fails the person navigating by it, worked through on Havenmark's filters and a mattress comparison table.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate whether a page's heading and landmark structure actually supports efficient navigation, not just valid markup
Predict how NVDA and VoiceOver announce table cells based on header association, and identify when that association is missing

contentSections.body: Havenmark's filter sidebar has five collapsible sections: Price, Material, Colour, Brand, Delivery time. Each one is marked up as an `<h3>` — semantically correct, WCAG 1.3.1 satisfied, an automated scan sees five properly nested headings and moves on. You open the Elements List, switch to the Headings tab, and see this instead of five distinct labels: "Filter," "Filter," "Filter," "Filter," "Filter." Every section header reads the visible chevron icon's alt text instead of the section name next to it. A sighted user glancing at the sidebar reads "Price," "Material," "Colour" without effort. Someone navigating by headings — the fastest way through a five-section sidebar for a screen reader user — hears the same word five times in a row and has to open every section to find out which one is which.

**Headings exist to be jumped between, not just read in order.** WCAG 2.4.6 (Headings and Labels) requires headings to *describe topic or purpose* — a heading that's structurally an `<h3>` in the right nesting position but says "Filter" five times over satisfies the letter of 1.3.1 (a heading exists, in the right hierarchy) while failing 2.4.6 outright, because none of the five identify anything. This is a distinction an automated scanner genuinely cannot make: checking that a heading element exists and has non-empty text is trivial; checking that its text actually distinguishes it from its siblings requires reading it.

**Landmarks are for skipping past whole regions, and need names when there's more than one of a kind.** `<nav>`, `<main>`, `<aside>`, `<header>`, `<footer>` each map to an ARIA landmark role automatically. A page with exactly one `<nav>` doesn't strictly need `aria-label` — NVDA announces it simply as "navigation." Havenmark's page has three: main site nav, the filter sidebar (also wrapped in `<nav>`, arguably a mismatch of intent but that's a separate issue), and a breadcrumb trail. Landing on any of the three with NVDA's `D` key or VoiceOver's Rotor Landmarks category announces "navigation" three times, with nothing to tell them apart — exactly the same failure shape as the identical headings, one level up in the structure. `aria-label="Filter product results"` on the sidebar's `<nav>` and `aria-label="Breadcrumb"` on the trail turn three identical stops into three that can be told apart before landing on them.

contentSections.scenario: You open NVDA's Elements List on Havenmark's product page and switch to the Landmarks tab. It lists: "navigation," "navigation," "navigation," "main." Underneath, in the Headings tab: "Filter," "Filter," "Filter," "Filter," "Filter," "Sofas."
contentSections.question: An automated scan of this page reports zero errors. What's the most accurate description of what's actually wrong?

options.label: The hierarchy and markup are technically valid, but none of the repeated labels let a user distinguish one stop from another before committing to open it — the failure is in the words, not the structure
The headings are at the wrong levels and need to be renumbered
The page is missing headings altogether, which is why the scan should have failed

feedback.identity-not-hierarchy: Correct. Five `<h3>` elements in a flat, consistent list under presumably one `<h2>` section is a valid, scannable hierarchy — that part of 1.3.1 genuinely passes. What fails is 2.4.6: none of the five headings, and none of the three navigation landmarks, describe what makes that particular one different from its siblings. A scanner checks for structure and non-empty text; it has no way to check whether "Filter" five times over is informative, because informativeness isn't a markup property.
feedback.wrong-heading-levels: There's no evidence of a level problem here — the scenario doesn't describe skipped levels or an h3 appearing before an h2. The actual defect is that five headings at a correct, valid level all say the identical word.
feedback.missing-headings-entirely: The headings exist — that's exactly why the automated scan passed and why this bug is hard to catch without listening to it. The problem is that they exist and are all identical, which a presence check can't detect.

contentSections.mechanism: Automated scanners verify markup properties: does a heading element exist, is it non-empty, does the nesting skip a level, does a landmark role resolve correctly. None of those checks can evaluate whether the text inside serves its purpose, because that's a judgment about meaning, not structure. The Elements List and Rotor exist precisely to surface this gap — they present exactly what a heading- or landmark-navigating user would see: a bare list of labels, stripped of visual context, which is the fastest way to notice when several of them collide.

contentSections.body:
**Tables are the sharpest version of this problem, because the failure isn't ambiguity — it's total loss of context on every cell.** Havenmark's mattress category page has a comparison table: rows are mattress models, columns are Firmness, Height, Trial period, Price. Built correctly, with `<th scope="col">` on each column header and `<th scope="row">` on each model name, NVDA moving cell to cell with `Ctrl+Alt+Right Arrow` announces something like: *"Firmness, column 2, Medium."* Every cell arrives with its column header attached, and if the row header is also marked up, the row identity too — so a user can drop into the middle of the table and immediately know what they're looking at.

Strip the `scope` attributes — leave the table visually identical, headers still bolded and still sitting in the first row and first column — and the exact same navigation announces just: *"Medium."* No column, no row, no idea whether that's a firmness rating, a delivery estimate, or a typo. The visual table and the announced table are built from the same HTML, but only one of them carries the header association, because `<th>` alone establishes a cell is a header — it does not by itself say *which* cells that header describes. `scope` (for simple tables) or `headers`/`id` pairs (for tables with a more complex structure, like merged cells or a two-level header row) are what make that connection explicit.

contentSections.scenario:
Havenmark's mattress table has 4 mattress models (rows) and 4 attribute columns (Firmness, Height, Trial period, Price), plus a header row and a header column — a 5×5 grid of cells including headers. It's marked up correctly with `<th scope="col">` on the four column headers and `<th scope="row">` on each model name.

A user moves with `Ctrl+Alt+Right Arrow` from the top-left header cell straight across the header row, then wraps to the start of the first data row and continues across it.
contentSections.question: How many `Ctrl+Alt+Right Arrow` presses does it take to go from the top-left cell to the last cell of the first data row (Price, first mattress)?
contentSections.explanation:
The header row has 5 cells (the empty corner cell, then Firmness, Height, Trial period, Price) — 4 presses to cross it after starting on the corner cell. Wrapping into the first data row lands on the row header (the mattress model name) with the 5th press, then Firmness, Height, Trial period, Price take presses 6, 7, 8. Total: 8.

The number itself matters less than what NVDA says at press 8: with scope attributes present, it announces something like "Price, column 5, 649 euro" — carrying both the column header and the row's model name forward automatically, because both were captured when scope was set. Strip scope from this same table and press 8 announces only "649 euro" — the number is real, but nothing ties it to Price, or to which mattress. The cell count doesn't change; what a screen reader user can do with each cell does.

contentSections.scenario: You're reviewing four table implementations in Havenmark's codebase for correct header association before recommending which pass as-is.

items.label: A one-header-row table with scope="col" on each <th> in the header row
A table with scope="col" on column headers and scope="row" on the first cell of each data row
A two-tier header table (grouped columns) using headers/id attribute pairs on every data cell
A table with header cells marked up as plain <td> styled bold and larger via CSS
A table using <th> for every header cell but with no scope attribute set anywhere
A table with a <caption> describing its contents, but plain <td> cells throughout including the header row

contentSections.question: Select every table that correctly associates data cells with their headers for a screen reader.

explanation.simple-scope-col: Correctly associated. For a table with one row of column headers and no row headers, scope="col" alone is sufficient — every cell in that column inherits the association.
explanation.row-and-col-scope: Correctly associated, and the strongest simple pattern — every cell in the table gets both its column and row identity announced, which is what made the mattress table example work.
explanation.headers-id: Correctly associated. This is the pattern for tables scope can't fully describe — grouped or two-tier headers — where each data cell explicitly lists the id of every header cell that applies to it.
explanation.bold-css-only: Not associated. Bold, larger text is a purely visual convention. Nothing in the accessibility tree marks these cells as headers at all — a screen reader announces them as ordinary data cells identical to every other <td>, and cell navigation carries no header context whatsoever.
explanation.th-no-scope: Not reliably associated. <th> alone correctly marks a cell as a header — screen readers will usually get simple single-row-header, single-column-header tables right by inferring position — but that inference breaks down on anything more complex, and scope removes the guesswork rather than depending on it. Without scope, treat this as unverified until tested directly.
explanation.caption-only: Not associated. A caption announces the table's overall purpose once, on entry — genuinely useful, and worth having — but it says nothing about any individual cell. Every cell-to-cell navigation afterward is exactly as context-free as if the caption didn't exist.

contentSections.synthesis: Three of the six actually connect a cell to what it means; three don't, for three different reasons — no markup at all, an incomplete signal that works by luck on simple structures, and a table-level description mistaken for a cell-level one. The check that separates them isn't reading the HTML for a <th> tag — it's the same one from the mattress table: navigate the table with Ctrl+Alt+Arrow keys yourself and listen for whether each cell announces where it lives.

contentSections.body: One more form-adjacent structure worth naming here, because it's the third repeat of the same underlying failure at yet another scale: `<fieldset>` and `<legend>` group related form controls — Havenmark's delivery-address form has a `<fieldset>` around Country, Postcode, and City with a `<legend>Delivery address</legend>`. Screen readers announce the legend once when you enter the group, then repeat it as context on the first field inside — so a user tabbing to the Postcode field hears "Delivery address, Postcode, edit" rather than just "Postcode, edit," which matters enormously when a page has both a delivery address and a billing address section using visually similar fields with identical field names.

A heading, a landmark, and a table header can each be structurally correct and still fail the person navigating by them, because none of the three checks that matter — does this label distinguish itself from its siblings, does this cell carry its header when you land on it — are things an automated scan can verify. All three require the same test: navigate by that structure yourself, using the Elements List, the Rotor, or Ctrl+Alt+Arrow through a table, and listen for whether what gets announced is actually enough to act on.

title: Forms, Errors, and the Live Region That Won't Shut Up
description: A live region that announces every keystroke, an error message a screen reader never connects to its field, and the difference between polite and assertive — worked through on Havenmark's cart quantity stepper and checkout validation.

learningObjectives.text: Diagnose why a live region announces too often or too rarely, and correct the trigger and politeness level
Verify that a form validation error is announced to the screen reader user at the moment it becomes relevant, not just visible on screen

contentSections.body: Havenmark's cart page has a quantity field per item — a plain `<input type="number">` — wired to an `aria-live="polite"` region below it that updates the running cart total. You tab to the quantity field for a €38 cushion, currently set to 1, and type "12" to order a dozen for a client's waiting room. NVDA announces: "Cart total, 38 euro... Cart total, 114 euro... Cart total, 342 euro." Three separate interruptions, one per digit as the number field's value changes from 1 to 1-then-12's intermediate states, each one cutting across whatever you were about to do next. By the time you've typed two characters you've heard three prices you didn't ask for, none of them final, and you still have to confirm you actually landed on 12 and not something the rapid announcements talked over.

**Live regions exist so a screen reader user learns about a change they didn't cause by navigating there.** `aria-live="polite"` — Havenmark's cart total is a reasonable use of it in principle — tells NVDA and VoiceOver to announce the region's new content once the user pauses, without cutting off whatever they're currently doing. `aria-live="assertive"` (and its shorthand, `role="alert"`) interrupts immediately, which is appropriate for something the user needs *right now* — a session-timeout warning, a payment failure — and wrong for almost everything else, because an assertive region talks over the user mid-keystroke every single time it fires, with no pause to wait for.

The cart total in the hook is marked `polite`, correctly. The bug isn't the politeness level — it's the trigger. The region updates on every keystroke inside the number field, which means it fires three times for a two-character edit, and each firing queues an announcement NVDA will eventually get to, whether or not the value has settled. The fix isn't a louder or quieter live region; it's firing it less often — on blur, or debounced until typing pauses for a beat, so the user hears one accurate total instead of three transient ones.

contentSections.scenario: Havenmark's cart total live region, marked aria-live="polite", updates its text content on every `input` event of the quantity field — meaning once per keystroke, not once per completed edit.
contentSections.question: What's the actual defect, and what fixes it?

options.label: The live region fires on every keystroke instead of on completed input — switch the trigger to fire on blur or after typing pauses, not on every keystroke; the politeness level itself is fine
The region should be assertive so each announcement finishes before the next keystroke
The cart total shouldn't be a live region at all — screen reader users should have to navigate to it manually

feedback.trigger-too-frequent: Correct. Polite is the right politeness level for a running total someone didn't ask about mid-typing — the problem is how often the content actually changes, not how the changes get announced. Firing on blur (when the field loses focus, meaning the user has moved on) or after a short pause in typing collapses three announcements of intermediate, throwaway values into one announcement of the number the user actually meant.
feedback.should-be-assertive: This makes the experience worse, not better — assertive announcements interrupt immediately rather than queuing politely, so three assertive interruptions during a two-character edit would cut across the user's typing three separate times instead of waiting for a pause. Politeness level was never the axis this bug lives on.
feedback.remove-live-region: This overcorrects a firing-frequency bug into losing real functionality. A running cart total that updates without requiring the user to navigate away and back is genuinely useful — sighted users get it for free by glancing at the screen. The fix is making it fire at the right moment, not removing it.

contentSections.mechanism: A live region's politeness level controls how an announcement competes with what the user is already doing — wait for a pause, or interrupt now. It says nothing about how often the region should update its content in the first place. A live region that fires on every keystroke will pester at exactly the same rate whether it's polite or assertive; the fix always lives at the trigger — what event causes the content to change — not at the aria-live value.

contentSections.body:
**Form errors are a live-region problem wearing different clothes: the announcement has to happen at the moment it's relevant, and it has to be connected to the field it's about.** Havenmark's checkout has a postcode field that validates on blur. A common, half-correct implementation: red border appears, an error message renders visually below the field — "Enter a valid postcode" — and nothing else happens. A sighted user sees the red border and the new text the instant it appears. A screen reader user who has already tabbed past the field to Address Line 2 hears none of it, because inserting text into the DOM doesn't announce itself; nothing pointed a live region or focus at the new content, so it sits there, visible and silent, until the user happens to tab backward and re-encounters the field.

Two fixes, and they solve different halves of the problem. First: `aria-describedby` on the postcode input, pointing at the error message's id, so that whenever the field *is* focused — including if the user tabs back to fix it — the error text gets read as part of the field's description, right after the field's name and value. Second, if the error needs to interrupt *at the moment it appears* rather than only when the field is later revisited: wrap the error in a `role="alert"` (implicitly assertive) so it announces itself the instant it's inserted, without requiring the user to be on that field at all. Real checkout forms usually need both — assertive announcement at the moment of the error, and a persistent describedby link for whenever the user returns to the field to fix it.

contentSections.scenario: Havenmark's checkout postcode field validates on blur. You're reviewing four candidate implementations for how the error gets communicated to a screen reader user.
contentSections.question: Select every implementation where a screen reader user is told about the error without having to stumble onto it by accident.

items.label: Error text rendered inside a role="alert" container the moment validation fails
Error text linked via aria-describedby on the input, no live region
role="alert" on first appearance, plus aria-describedby linking it to the field permanently
A red border and red error text, no ARIA connecting either to the field or announcing them
The error message set as the input's title attribute only
Validation failure logged to the browser console for developers to review

explanation.role-alert-only: Tells the user, at the moment it happens. An alert region announces itself as soon as its content is inserted, interrupting whatever the user is doing — appropriate here because the user needs to know the field they just left didn't validate.
explanation.describedby-only: Tells the user, but only when they're on the field. If they don't return to it, this alone never announces anything — it's a real fix for one situation and a partial one for the other.
explanation.both: Covers both situations: the alert announces the failure the instant it happens, even if the user has already tabbed onward, and the describedby link means the message is still there, attached to the field, whenever they come back to fix it.
explanation.visual-red-border-only: Tells no one who isn't looking at the screen. Colour and unlinked text convey nothing to the accessibility tree — this is functionally identical to no error message existing, for anyone using a screen reader.
explanation.title-attribute: Tells almost no one. title text is inconsistently and often not announced by screen readers at all, is never visible without hovering, and specifically fails as an error mechanism because it isn't tied to the moment the error occurs — a user has to already suspect there's a problem and go looking.
explanation.console-log: Tells no user anything. This is a developer-facing artifact, invisible to anyone operating the actual page, sighted or not.

contentSections.synthesis: One approach handles the moment the error occurs, one handles the field being revisited later, and the strongest checkout forms use both because a real user's session includes both situations — the field they just left, and the field they come back to after reading a summary of what needs fixing. Everything that isn't ARIA-connected to the field or announced at the right moment tells a screen reader user nothing at all, no matter how obvious it looks on screen.

contentSections.code: Enter a valid Dutch postcode (1234 AB)
contentSections.question: This looks like the correct pattern — aria-describedby is there, pointing at the right element. What still goes wrong for a screen reader user?

options.label: aria-describedby only re-announces when the field regains focus — a user who's already moved past it hears nothing at the moment the error appears
The id doesn't match between the input and the span
display:none permanently removes the span from the accessibility tree, so describedby points at nothing

feedback.static-describedby-not-live: Correct. aria-describedby is a static association — it tells a screen reader "when this field is focused, also read this other element's text." It is not a live region and announces nothing on its own when the referenced content changes while focus is elsewhere. Here, focus moves to the next field the instant blur fires, and validation runs after that — so the error text appears while the user is already on Address Line 2, and describedby only helps if and when they tab back to Postcode.
feedback.wrong-id: The ids match exactly — postcode-error on the span, aria-describedby="postcode-error" on the input. That part of the wiring is correct; the failure is about timing, not the reference itself.
feedback.display-none-breaks-association: display:none does hide content from the accessibility tree while it's set — but the script here removes it (display:inline) at the exact moment the error becomes real, so by the time there's an error to announce, the span is visible and in the tree. The gap is that becoming visible in the tree doesn't itself trigger an announcement.

contentSections.flawExplanation: aria-describedby answers "what should I also tell the user about this field, next time they're on it" — it never answers "tell the user about this right now, wherever they are." A field that validates on blur, by definition, has already lost focus by the time the error text exists, which means the describedby link alone will silently miss every first-time error unless the field also gets a role="alert" (or the error text is placed inside one) to announce itself at the moment of insertion. This is the same class of bug as the mid-typing live region earlier in this lesson: correct markup, wrong assumption about when a screen reader actually re-reads something.

contentSections.body: A live region and a form error share the same two questions: how often should this actually interrupt someone, and will the person hear it at the moment it becomes true, or only if they happen to be standing in the right place? Politeness level answers the first question. aria-describedby alone never answers the second — that needs an alert, or a live region, firing at the moment the content changes.

title: Keyboard-Only Checkout: Focus Order, Focus Visibility, and the Trap Nobody Meant to Build
description: A checkout combobox with roving tabindex, a focus ring that's technically present but invisible against Havenmark's blue buttons, and a payment-step accordion that quietly traps focus — three keyboard failures a mouse-driven review would never surface.

learningObjectives.text: Operate a composite widget (combobox, accordion) using only the keyboard and identify whether its focus management matches the expected pattern
Evaluate whether a focus indicator meets WCAG's visibility and non-obscurement requirements, not just whether one exists

contentSections.body: Havenmark's checkout has an address autocomplete field — start typing "1017" and a listbox of matching Amsterdam postcodes drops down. Put your mouse aside and try it with a keyboard alone: type the digits, press Down Arrow to highlight the first suggestion, press Down Arrow again to move to the second. Nothing visibly changes on screen except a subtle background shade you'd need to be staring at the right pixel to catch — and if you're using NVDA, nothing gets announced at all between the two Down Arrow presses. Press Enter. The field fills with the *first* suggestion, not the one you thought you'd moved to. The widget is tracking your arrow presses internally, but never told you, sighted or not, which option currently had your attention.

**A combobox with a listbox popup manages "active" state without moving real keyboard focus — and has to announce that state explicitly, or the whole widget lies to you.** Keyboard focus stays on the text input the entire time; arrow keys move a visual and programmatic "active descendant" indicator among the listbox options instead of literally tabbing between them, because moving real focus off the input would lose your typed characters and break the ability to keep typing to filter further. The mechanism that's supposed to carry this: `aria-activedescendant` on the input, updated to the `id` of the currently-highlighted option on every arrow press. When it's wired correctly, NVDA and VoiceOver announce the option's text and its position ("1017 AB, 1 of 4") every time you arrow to a new one — because a screen reader watches that attribute specifically to know an active-descendant selection changed, and announces it the same way it would announce landing on a genuinely-focused element. Havenmark's version updates the highlight in CSS but never touches `aria-activedescendant`, so nothing gets announced, and Enter falls back to whatever the first result happened to be, because there was never a communicated, agreed-on "currently selected" option to submit.

**This is a different failure from the roving-tabindex pattern used in genuinely focus-moving composite widgets** — a filter chip list, for instance, where Left/Right Arrow moves *real* focus between chips, each one `tabindex="-1"` except the currently active one at `tabindex="0"`. There, arrow keys do move literal focus, and the browser's own focus-change announcement carries the update for free. The combobox pattern and the roving-tabindex pattern solve related problems — "let arrow keys move between a set of related options without adding every option to the page's Tab sequence" — with genuinely different mechanisms, and mixing them up (using `aria-activedescendant` semantics but expecting focus events, or vice versa) is exactly how a widget like Havenmark's address field ships broken.

contentSections.scenario: Havenmark's address-suggestion combobox highlights the active option with a CSS class on arrow-key press, but never sets aria-activedescendant on the input, and never moves literal keyboard focus onto the listbox options.
contentSections.question: Why does this specific combination of choices mean nothing gets announced when the user arrows between suggestions?

options.label: Neither of the two mechanisms that would trigger an announcement is present — focus never literally moves (so there's no focus-change event to announce), and aria-activedescendant is never set (so there's no active-descendant change for the screen reader to detect either)
The listbox is missing role="listbox", which is the only thing that would cause announcements
Using a CSS class to highlight the option overrides and disables any ARIA state on the same element

feedback.no-activedescendant-no-focus-move: Correct. A screen reader announces a new selection through exactly one of two channels: real focus landing on a new element, or aria-activedescendant changing to point at a new id while the input itself stays focused. Havenmark's implementation does neither — focus never leaves the text input, and nothing updates aria-activedescendant — so from the accessibility tree's point of view, absolutely nothing happened when the user pressed Down Arrow twice, even though the screen visibly changed.
feedback.listbox-role-missing: role="listbox" on the popup and role="option" on each item matter for identifying what kind of widget this is once you do land on it — but they don't by themselves cause an announcement on arrow-key press. The missing piece is specifically the activedescendant wiring (or, in the alternative pattern, real focus movement), not the container roles.
feedback.css-classes-block-aria: A CSS class and an ARIA attribute are entirely independent — applying one never disables the other. The bug here is that aria-activedescendant was never set in the first place, not that a class is somehow interfering with it.

contentSections.mechanism: A combobox-with-listbox widget has to choose one of two focus-management strategies and implement it completely: either move real DOM focus between listbox options (rare for this pattern, since it usually breaks continued typing), or keep focus on the input and drive aria-activedescendant to point at whichever option id is currently highlighted. A screen reader only reacts to one of those two signals — it cannot infer "something changed" from a CSS class alone, because a CSS class carries no meaning in the accessibility tree at all.

contentSections.body:
**Focus visibility is the other half of keyboard testing, and it fails in a way an automated scan structurally cannot catch: it's a rendering judgment, not a markup one.** WCAG 2.4.7 (Focus Visible, Level AA) requires that any keyboard-operable interface have a visible indicator when an element has focus. Havenmark's "Add to basket" button is a case that technically has a focus outline — `outline: 2px solid #1a5fb4` — sitting on a button whose own background is `#1a5fb4`. The outline exists in the DOM, exists in the CSS, and would show up fine against a white or grey background. Against its own button's fill colour, it's invisible: same hue, same lightness, functionally the same pixel. A keyboard user tabs onto the button and has no visual signal that they're now on it — they'd have to tab one further step and watch what *loses* focus to infer, backward, where they just were.

WCAG 2.2 sharpened this further with 2.4.11 (Focus Not Obscured – Minimum, Level AA): a focus indicator has to not be entirely hidden by other content — a sticky header covering the top of the viewport that fully obscures a focused element scrolled underneath it is a 2.4.11 failure even if the indicator itself, in isolation, would have been perfectly visible. Both criteria point at the same practical test: tab through the page and, at every stop, ask "could I, right now, point to exactly where focus is without already knowing the tab order" — not "does the CSS declare an outline."

contentSections.intro: Assemble a working, keyboard-honest version of Havenmark's address combobox. Three decisions.

fields.prompt: Where does keyboard focus live while arrowing through suggestions?

options.label: Stays on the text input the whole time
options.value: stays on the text input the whole time

options.label: Moves onto each listbox option as it's highlighted
options.value: moves onto each listbox option as it's highlighted

options.label: Moves to the listbox container itself, once, on first arrow press
options.value: moves to the listbox container itself, once, on first arrow press

fields.correctValue: stays on the text input the whole time

feedback.stays on the text input the whole time: Right — this is what lets the user keep typing to narrow the list further while still moving a highlight among the results. It's exactly why aria-activedescendant exists: to carry the "which option is active" information without literal focus ever leaving the input.
feedback.moves onto each listbox option as it's h: This is a valid pattern for some composite widgets, but it breaks a combobox specifically — the moment focus leaves the input, the user loses the ability to keep typing characters to filter, which is the entire point of a type-ahead suggestion list.
feedback.moves to the listbox container itself, o: This produces exactly the bug from the hook: focus parks somewhere generic, individual option selection is tracked by something other than focus, and nothing communicates which specific option is active.

fields.prompt: How does the currently-highlighted option get communicated to a screen reader?

options.label: aria-activedescendant on the input, updated on every arrow press
options.value: aria-activedescendant on the input, updated on every arrow press

options.label: A CSS class change on the highlighted option
options.value: a CSS class change on the highlighted option

options.label: aria-live="polite" region announcing the option's text
options.value: aria-live region announcing the option's text

fields.correctValue: aria-activedescendant on the input, updated on every arrow press

feedback.aria-activedescendant on the input, upda: Right — this is the mechanism a screen reader specifically watches for on this pattern, and it fires the same kind of announcement a real focus change would, without requiring focus to actually move.
feedback.a CSS class change on the highlighted op: This is the bug from the hook. A class carries zero meaning to the accessibility tree — it changes pixels and nothing else.
feedback.aria-live region announcing the option's: This can technically work, but it's a mismatch for this pattern and introduces the exact per-keystroke-noise problem from the previous lesson's cart total — arrowing rapidly through five options would queue five separate announcements rather than giving the standard, expected "selection changed" behaviour aria-activedescendant provides for free.

options.label: Whichever option aria-activedescendant currently points at
options.value: whichever option aria-activedescendant currently points at

options.label: Always the first option in the list
options.value: always the first option in the list

options.label: Whatever the mouse is currently hovering, if anything
options.value: whatever the mouse is currently hovering

fields.correctValue: whichever option aria-activedescendant currently points at

feedback.whichever option aria-activedescendant c: Right. This closes the loop — the same value driving what's announced is also the value driving what gets selected, so what the user was told is highlighted is what they actually get.
feedback.always the first option in the list: This is Havenmark's actual bug: Enter ignoring arrow-key state entirely and always submitting the first result, regardless of how many times the user pressed Down.
feedback.whatever the mouse is currently hovering: A keyboard-only user has no mouse position to speak of, so this either selects nothing or selects an arbitrary leftover hover state from before they started using the keyboard — neither is a coherent answer to "what did the user just choose."

contentSections.synthesis: One mechanism, aria-activedescendant, has to do three jobs at once: track internally which option is active, tell the screen reader what changed, and agree with whatever Enter actually submits. Havenmark's version skipped the mechanism entirely and improvised three separate, disconnected answers to those three jobs — a CSS class, silence, and "always the first one" — which is why it looked like it worked to anyone testing with a mouse and eyes, and fell apart completely for anyone who couldn't see the highlight.

contentSections.question: You're testing Havenmark's checkout for keyboard traps before sign-off. Put these checks in the order that catches a trap fastest, rather than discovering it by accident forty tabs in.
steps: Tab forward through the entire checkout flow once, end to end, noting anywhere Tab stops responding
At any composite widget (combobox, accordion, date picker), test its documented keyboard pattern specifically — arrow keys, Escape, Enter
At any modal or overlay within checkout, tab past the last element and confirm focus wraps rather than escaping
Shift+Tab backward through the same flow, since a trap can exist in only one direction
Note every stop where the visible focus indicator was not clearly identifiable against its background
contentSections.explanation: A full forward pass first, because a trap that stops you cold is the highest-severity finding and you want to know immediately whether one exists before spending time on subtler checks. Testing each composite widget's specific pattern comes next and deliberately after the full pass, not interleaved with it — interrupting a straight-through tab pass to deep-dive every widget as you reach it makes it easy to lose track of whether you've actually covered the whole flow. Modal-specific wrap-checking is its own step because a trap inside a dialog is a different mechanism than a trap in the page flow, and both need verifying independently. Shift+Tab backward is listed separately, deliberately, because a trap built only for the forward direction is common and easy to miss if you only ever test one way through. Focus-visibility notes come last because they're findings you can collect as a byproduct of the passes above, without needing a dedicated pass of their own — but they still need to be written down as you go, not reconstructed afterward from memory.

contentSections.body: A composite widget that manages selection without moving real focus has to say so out loud through aria-activedescendant, or a screen reader hears nothing while the screen visibly changes. A focus indicator that exists in the CSS but disappears against its own background, or gets covered by a sticky header, fails 2.4.7 and 2.4.11 exactly as completely as no indicator at all — the check is always "can I see or hear where focus is, right now," never "is there a rule in the stylesheet."

title: 200%, 400%, and the Settings Underneath: Reflow, Reduced Motion, Forced Colors
description: Zooming Havenmark's checkout to 400% doesn't magnify the page the way a magnifier does — it demands reflow. Reduced-motion and forced-colors preferences are two more OS-level settings a real audit has to test against, not assume away.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish browser zoom with reflow from OS-level screen magnification and identify which failure mode each produces
Verify a page's behaviour under prefers-reduced-motion and forced-colors rather than assuming default styling degrades gracefully

contentSections.body: Set your browser to 400% zoom (`Ctrl/Cmd` and `+`, repeatedly, or set it directly in the zoom menu) on Havenmark's checkout page and look at the payment step. At 100%, three payment method cards sit in a row: iDEAL, credit card, PayPal. At 400%, on an ordinary 1280px-wide laptop viewport, those three cards are still trying to sit in a row — which at 400% zoom means the page has to be roughly 5120 logical pixels wide to contain them at their original proportions, and your browser window is nowhere near that. The result: a horizontal scrollbar appears at the bottom of the page, and reading the payment options means scrolling right to see the middle card, then right again for the third, then all the way back left to reach the field above them. Nothing crashed. Nothing is technically hidden. It is simply unusable at a zoom level WCAG explicitly requires supporting without two-dimensional scrolling.

**Two separate WCAG success criteria govern magnification, and they test differently.** WCAG 1.4.4 (Resize Text, Level AA) requires that text can be resized up to 200% without loss of content or functionality, using the browser's own zoom — not a special assistive tool. WCAG 1.4.10 (Reflow, Level AA) goes further: at a zoom equivalent to a 320 CSS-pixel-wide viewport (roughly 400% zoom on a 1280px-wide starting point), content must reflow into a single column with no horizontal scrolling required to read it — except for content that's inherently two-dimensional, like a data table, an image, or a map, which are explicitly exempted. Havenmark's three-card payment row is a textbook 1.4.10 failure: nothing about a row of three simple option cards requires two-dimensional layout, it's just fixed-width flexbox that never got a responsive breakpoint for extreme zoom, and the visual result — needing to scroll both down *and* right to read a payment form — is exactly the failure 1.4.10 exists to prevent.

**Browser zoom and OS-level screen magnification are not the same accommodation, and testing only one tells you nothing about the other.** Browser zoom (what you just tested) reflows the page's own layout — text rewraps, columns can stack, the DOM itself adapts if the CSS is responsive. A screen magnifier — Windows Magnifier, macOS Zoom, or third-party tools like ZoomText, common among low-vision users who need more optical magnification than browser zoom alone provides — instead takes a snapshot of the rendered page at its normal size and pans a viewport lens over it, the way a physical magnifying glass moves over a printed page. Nothing reflows; the layout stays exactly as designed, just enlarged and cropped to whatever fits in the lens. This produces a completely different failure mode: not horizontal scrolling, but *losing context* — a magnifier user panned in on the "Continue to payment" button has no peripheral view of the rest of the page, so a validation error that appeared elsewhere on the page, outside the current pan position, can go completely unseen even though it's fully visible to anyone not currently zoomed in on a different corner of the screen.

contentSections.scenario: Havenmark's checkout, zoomed to 400% in the browser (not a screen magnifier), on a standard 1280px-wide viewport. The three payment-method cards are laid out with display: flex and a fixed min-width per card, no responsive breakpoint.
contentSections.question: What's the correct diagnosis, and which WCAG criterion does it map to?

options.label: This is a 1.4.10 Reflow failure — the fixed-width flex row forces two-dimensional scrolling at a zoom level the criterion explicitly requires supporting without it, for content that isn't inherently tabular or image-based
This is only a 1.4.4 Resize Text failure, about the text being too small to read
This isn't a failure — payment method selection counts as the kind of two-dimensional content 1.4.10 exempts

feedback.reflow-failure-1410: Correct. The text itself is perfectly legible at 400% — that's 1.4.4 doing its job. The problem is layout: a row of three cards refusing to stack into a single column forces horizontal scrolling to read content that has no structural reason to need two-dimensional space, which is precisely the failure 1.4.10 targets.
feedback.resize-text-failure-only: The text is readable — arguably too large in places, but not the actual complaint here. The user can read every word; they just can't see all three payment options without scrolling in two directions to find them, which is a layout problem, not a text-legibility one.
feedback.not-a-failure-exempt-content: The 1.4.10 exemption is for content genuinely requiring two-dimensional presentation to remain meaningful — a data table where losing the column alignment would lose the data's meaning, a floor plan, a map. Three payment method options in a row are exempt from nothing; they're a design choice that could stack into a single column with zero loss of meaning, which is exactly the responsive behaviour the criterion is asking for.

contentSections.mechanism: 1.4.10 targets layouts that were built assuming a fixed, generous viewport width and never given a responsive path for when that assumption breaks — exactly the situation a fixed min-width flex row creates. The fix is the same one already needed for a narrow phone screen: let the cards stack vertically below a width threshold. A layout responsive enough for mobile is very often, though not automatically, also reflow-compliant at high zoom, because both are the same underlying requirement approached from two different trigger conditions — a narrow physical viewport, or a zoomed-in effective one.

contentSections.body:
**Two more OS-level preferences round out this category, and both are things Havenmark's site can query and respond to — or ignore, at real cost.**

`prefers-reduced-motion` reflects a setting the user turned on deliberately — macOS System Settings › Accessibility › Display › Reduce Motion, or Windows Settings › Accessibility › Visual effects › Animation effects — usually because motion triggers vestibular symptoms, migraine, or genuine nausea, not because they find it merely distracting. Havenmark's checkout has a progress bar that animates its fill with a spring-bounce effect on every step change; wrapping that animation in a `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` block that swaps it for an instant, non-bouncing fill respects the setting directly. WCAG 2.3.3 (Animation from Interactions, Level AAA) asks for exactly this: motion triggered by an interaction should be disable-able. It's AAA, not AA — meaning it's not a strict conformance requirement at the AA level most engagements target — but a mid-size retailer with a checkout flow experiencing real cart abandonment has a business reason to honour it that has nothing to do with the conformance level, since the population affected is exactly the population currently leaving the animated version of that page.

`forced-colors: active` fires when a user has a Windows contrast theme enabled — a system-wide setting, not a browser one, that remaps the entire page to a small, user-chosen palette (`Canvas`, `CanvasText`, `LinkText`, `ButtonText`, `ButtonFace`, `Highlight`, `HighlightText`, `GrayText`) and overrides most author-specified colours outright. This is where background images and background-colour-only UI cues disappear completely: an "Add to basket" button styled with a background colour and *no border* renders as a borderless, background-less shape in forced-colors mode, because the background colour is exactly the kind of author styling forced-colors overrides — leaving the button either invisible or reduced to unstyled text with no way to tell where its clickable boundary is. WCAG 1.4.11 (Non-text Contrast, Level AA) requires UI component boundaries to have 3:1 contrast against adjacent colours in normal rendering; testing under forced-colors specifically catches the version of this bug that only appears once a user's contrast theme has already stripped away every colour the button was relying on to look like a button.

contentSections.scenario: You're testing Havenmark's "Add to basket" button under Windows forced-colors mode (a contrast theme enabled). In normal rendering it has a solid blue background, white text, and no explicit border.
contentSections.question: Select every outcome that's a genuine, expected consequence of forced-colors mode being active — not a bug specific to this button.

items.label: The blue background colour is replaced by the user's chosen Canvas colour
The white button text is replaced by the user's chosen ButtonText colour
An explicit border, if one had been declared, would generally still render using a forced-colors-appropriate colour rather than being stripped entirely
The button stops being clickable while forced-colors is active
The button's text becomes fully invisible, with no colour at all
The page fails to render at all under forced-colors mode

explanation.bg-color-overridden: Genuinely expected. Forced-colors mode exists specifically to replace author background colours with the user's chosen palette — that's the feature working as intended, for a user who has decided the operating system's contrast, not the website's, gets final say.
explanation.text-recolored: Genuinely expected, for the same reason — text colour is one of the properties forced-colors mode is designed to override.
explanation.author-border-honoured-if-present: Genuinely expected, and this is the detail that turns forced-colors from a problem into a solution: a border you declared explicitly still renders, remapped to a system colour, giving the button a visible boundary even after its background is gone. This is exactly why the button in this scenario, which has no explicit border, ends up with no visible boundary at all — there was nothing for forced-colors to preserve.
explanation.button-becomes-unclickable: Not accurate. Forced-colors mode changes rendering, not interactivity — the button remains fully clickable and keyboard-operable. The failure here is purely visual: a user can't tell where to click, not that clicking stops working.
explanation.text-disappears-completely: Not accurate as a blanket outcome. Forced-colors mode recolors text to a system value like ButtonText — the text itself generally stays visible, just in a different colour than the author chose. Total invisibility of text isn't the typical failure this mode produces.
explanation.page-fails-to-load: Not accurate. Forced-colors mode is a rendering and styling change applied by the browser, not a mechanism that prevents pages from loading.

contentSections.synthesis: The button doesn't break because forced-colors mode is buggy — it breaks because the button's own styling never declared a border, relying entirely on a background colour that the mode is specifically designed to remove. The fix isn't fighting forced-colors mode; it's adding an explicit border so there's something for the mode to preserve. This is the same shape of finding as the modal in an earlier lesson relying on a backdrop that meant nothing to assistive tech: a visual cue with no structural backing disappears the instant the environment it was designed for changes.

contentSections.body: Browser zoom demands reflow — WCAG 1.4.10, no two-dimensional scrolling at roughly 400%, for content that isn't inherently tabular. A screen magnifier pans instead of reflowing, and its failure mode is losing context, not scrolling. Reduced motion and forced colors are both OS settings that override a page's own styling by design — testing under them catches the buttons and animations that were only ever styled for the default environment, not the one a real low-vision or motion-sensitive user is actually running.

title: Voice Control and Switch Access: When the Visible Word Is the Only Command That Works
description: Operating Havenmark's account page by saying the words on screen, and again by scanning through it one switch-press at a time — two access methods with almost nothing in common except that both are unforgiving of a mismatched label.

learningObjectives.text: Predict whether a voice control command will succeed based on whether the visible label matches the element's accessible name
Evaluate a page's usability under switch scanning by tracing its scan order and estimating switch-presses required per task

contentSections.body: You're testing Havenmark's account page with macOS Voice Control turned on — System Settings › Accessibility › Voice Control, then saying commands out loud. The page has a button reading "Save changes" in visible text. You say "Click Save changes." Nothing happens. You try "Show numbers," which overlays a number on every clickable element Voice Control can find — the button gets a number, you say it, and the click goes through. So the button was reachable; voice matching on its visible words just didn't work. Inspecting the markup: `<button aria-label="Submit account form">Save changes</button>`. The accessible name a screen reader announces, and the name voice control software matches spoken commands against, is "Submit account form" — a string that appears nowhere on the visible page, put there by a developer who assumed a more descriptive aria-label was strictly an improvement.

**Voice control software matches spoken commands against the accessible name, not the visible text — and when the two differ, the words a sighted user reads out loud simply do nothing.** macOS Voice Control, Windows Voice Access, and Dragon NaturallySpeaking (still common in enterprise and clinical settings, and among users with RSI or limited hand mobility who adopted it before the built-in OS tools matured) all work the same way at this layer: "Click [name]" looks for a control whose accessible name matches what was said, falling back to a numbered-overlay or grid-based mode (Voice Control's "Show numbers," Dragon's MouseGrid) only when no match is found. This is WCAG 2.5.3 (Label in Name, Level A) from an entirely operational angle — the criterion already covered in this track's foundations domain as a naming-consistency rule is, for a voice control user, the literal difference between a command working and a command doing nothing.

The fix is almost always to stop reaching for `aria-label` as a way to add detail. If "Save changes" needs more context for a screen reader user, `aria-describedby` pointing at nearby explanatory text adds a *description* without overriding the *name* — screen readers announce the name first, then the description, so nothing is lost, and voice control keeps matching against words that are actually on the screen. `aria-label` should only replace visible text when there genuinely is none to replace — an icon-only button, for instance — never as a way to say something different from what's already there.

contentSections.scenario: Havenmark's account page: <button aria-label="Submit account form">Save changes</button>. A Voice Control user says "Click Save changes."
contentSections.question: Why does this command fail, precisely?

options.label: Voice Control matches spoken commands against the accessible name — here, "Submit account form" from aria-label — not the visible text "Save changes" the user actually read and said
Voice Control can't reliably detect <button> elements at all, only links
The correct command phrasing would have been just "Save changes" without the word "Click"

feedback.matches-accessible-name-not-visible: Correct. Voice Control, Voice Access, and Dragon all build their command vocabulary from the accessibility tree — specifically the accessible name, computed with aria-label taking precedence over visible text when both are present. "Submit account form" is what the software is listening for; "Save changes" is the word the user actually read off the screen and said, and it was never in the running.
feedback.voice-control-cant-see-buttons: Voice Control detects buttons reliably — that's exactly why "Show numbers" successfully overlaid a number on this one. The button was found; the specific phrase spoken just didn't match the string voice control checks it against.
feedback.command-phrasing-wrong: Both "Click Save changes" and "Save changes" alone are valid, commonly supported phrasings across these tools, and neither would succeed here — the mismatch is in what string is being matched against, not in the command's grammar.

contentSections.mechanism: Voice control software builds its command vocabulary from the accessibility tree, the same source screen readers read from — which is precisely why WCAG 2.5.3 groups this under one rule ("where a control has visible text, the accessible name must contain that text") rather than treating screen reader users and voice control users as needing separate protections. They're protected by the exact same fix, because they're both reading the same underlying name-computation result — one by ear, one by mouth.

contentSections.body:
**Switch access replaces continuous pointing with a single binary signal, scanned across the page's interactive elements — and it inherits every keyboard-order problem this domain has already covered, at a much higher physical cost per mistake.** A switch user operates one or two physical switches — a button under a hand, a puff-activated sip-and-puff switch, a head switch — instead of a mouse or a full keyboard. In single-switch auto-scanning, the most common configuration, a highlight moves automatically from one focusable element to the next at a fixed interval (commonly one to several seconds, tuned to the individual), and pressing the switch selects whatever's currently highlighted; two-switch step-scanning replaces the automatic timer with one switch that manually advances the highlight and a second that selects, trading speed for less pressure to "catch" the right moment. iOS and iPadOS Switch Control and Android's Switch Access are the most mature built-in implementations; the scan order they walk is, in both cases, the same DOM/focus order a keyboard's Tab key would follow.

That inheritance is what makes every keyboard-order finding from earlier lessons in this domain a switch-access finding too, automatically — a navigation landmark placed late in the DOM costs a keyboard user extra Tab presses, which is an inconvenience measured in seconds; it costs a switch user the same number of *scan cycles*, each one a deliberate, physically effortful wait-and-press, which is a cost measured in real fatigue. A checkout flow that takes 15 Tab presses for a keyboard user to complete can easily mean 60-plus scan-and-select cycles for a single-switch user, once every intermediate stop the scanner has to pass through on its way there is counted. This is also exactly where WCAG 2.2.1 (Timing Adjustable, Level A) stops being an abstract requirement: a session timeout or an auto-advancing carousel tuned for a mouse user's pace can run out entirely before a slow, deliberate switch scan even reaches the control it needs.

contentSections.scenario: Havenmark's account page has a "Change password" section reachable via: skip link, main nav (6 links), breadcrumb (2 links), a promotional banner dismiss button, page heading (not focusable), then finally the account sidebar with "Change password" as its 4th of 6 links.
contentSections.question: For a single-switch auto-scanning user with a 2-second scan interval, roughly how much does DOM position — rather than task complexity — cost them to simply reach the "Change password" link, before they've done anything with it yet?

options.label: A real, meaningful cost — likely 10+ scan cycles and 20+ seconds before reaching the link at all, none of which reflects any difficulty in the actual task of changing a password
Negligible — scanning is designed to make position irrelevant to the user's experience
This is a keyboard-specific concern and doesn't apply to switch scanning, which uses a different mechanism entirely

feedback.meaningful-real-cost: Correct, and worth actually counting: skip link (1), 6 nav links (2-7), 2 breadcrumb links (8-9), 1 dismiss button (10), then into the sidebar to reach the 4th link (11-14) — roughly 14 scan stops before the target, at 2 seconds each attention-and-decide cycle even before pressing, near half a minute spent entirely on reaching the task, for a task (changing a password) that has nothing to do with any of the 13 stops passed along the way.
feedback.negligible-cost: This gets the mechanism backwards — auto-scanning makes position matter *more*, not less, because every single intermediate stop costs a full scan interval whether or not the user has any interest in it. A keyboard user can Tab past irrelevant stops quickly; a scanning user has to wait through each one at the same fixed pace.
feedback.only-affects-keyboard-users: Switch scanning walks the same underlying focus order a keyboard's Tab key follows — that's precisely why it's affected by DOM position at all, and why every focus-order finding in this domain doubles as a switch-access finding, just at a steeper physical cost.

contentSections.concept: Scan order is Tab order, restated at a pace the user doesn't control. A page can be entirely keyboard-operable — every element reachable, focus order logical, no traps — and still impose a real, countable cost on a switch user purely from how many stops sit between the page's start and the task they came for. The practical implication for an audit: a landmark like the account sidebar, reachable in a couple of Tab presses for most users, is worth flagging for a heading-and-landmark skip mechanism (a "skip to account menu" link, or moving frequently-needed controls earlier in DOM order) specifically because of what it costs a scanning user, even when it barely registers for anyone else.

contentSections.body: Voice control fails silently on a mismatched accessible name — the fix is the same one as always: let the visible words be the name, and put anything extra in a description instead. Switch scanning fails on distance, not difficulty — it walks the exact scan order a keyboard's Tab key would, at a fixed pace the user can't speed up, so every stop between the page's start and the task the user actually came for is a real, physical cost worth counting, not just noting.

title: Building the AT Test Matrix: Which Combinations Earn Their Place
description: You cannot test every AT against every browser against every OS in a real engagement. Turning six lessons of hands-on behaviour into a defensible, prioritized AT test matrix for Havenmark's site — this domain's artefact.

learningObjectives.text: Select a defensible, prioritized set of AT/browser/OS combinations to test within a fixed engagement budget, and justify every inclusion and exclusion
Produce an AT test matrix that a client or reviewer could act on without further clarification

contentSections.body: Havenmark's project lead asks a fair question at the scoping call: "How many screen readers are you testing with?" The honest answer isn't a number pulled from a best-practices list — NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, TalkBack, and Narrator all exist, plus at least three browsers each, plus two magnification approaches, two voice control tools, and switch access, and the engagement has a fixed number of billable hours. Testing every combination isn't a rigor problem to solve with more hours; it's mathematically impossible to sell as a line item, and a client who's told "we test everything" is being sold a claim nobody actually intends to deliver on. The real deliverable isn't exhaustive coverage. It's a matrix that names exactly which combinations get tested, states why those and not others, and lets a client see the reasoning well enough to push back on it if they disagree.

**A defensible matrix is built from three things: real usage share, genuinely different interaction models, and the specific risk profile of the site being tested — not an attempt at completeness.** Usage share matters because testing choices should track where actual users are: the WebAIM Screen Reader User Survey has consistently found NVDA paired with either Firefox or Chrome as the most common desktop combination among people who use a screen reader daily, with JAWS still heavily represented, particularly in workplace and government contexts. VoiceOver isn't optional for a site with meaningful mobile traffic, for a reason that has nothing to do with popularity contests: it's the *only* screen reader available on iOS, so any site failing under VoiceOver on Safari has failed for effectively every blind iPhone user who visits it, full stop.

Interaction model matters more than raw combination count, because two tools with the same underlying model tend to surface the same bugs — testing NVDA and JAWS on the exact same Windows/Chrome pairing catches meaningfully less new ground than testing NVDA on Windows *and* VoiceOver on macOS, because NVDA and VoiceOver differ exactly the way this domain has spent six lessons on: browse/focus mode versus Quick Nav and interacting-with, different table navigation commands, different rotor and elements-list tooling. The same logic applies across every access method covered in this domain, not just screen readers — a keyboard-only pass, a 400% zoom reflow pass, a voice control pass, and a switch-scanning pass each catch a category of bug the others structurally cannot, because each one exercises a different mechanism for reaching and operating a control.

Risk profile is what makes the matrix specific to Havenmark rather than generic: a retail site's revenue-critical path is product discovery through checkout completion, so that path gets the deepest combination coverage, while a static "About us" page reasonably gets a single spot-check pass rather than the full matrix, because a failure there costs a browsing inconvenience and a failure in checkout costs a completed sale.
