contentSections.scenario: A junior QA engineer proposes testing Havenmark's checkout with NVDA+Chrome, NVDA+Firefox, NVDA+Edge, and JAWS+Chrome — four combinations, all screen readers, all Windows.
contentSections.question: What's the strongest critique of this proposal, given a fixed testing budget?

options.label: All four combinations share the same interaction model and the same OS — none of them would catch a VoiceOver-specific, keyboard-specific, magnification-specific, or voice-control-specific failure, which are categories of bug this domain has shown are structurally invisible to any screen reader test
Testing the same screen reader across three browsers is inherently wasteful and should never be done
JAWS has low enough usage share that it should be dropped entirely from any matrix

feedback.no-model-diversity: Correct. Four rows, one access method, one operating system — the budget is being spent entirely on browser-engine differences within NVDA and JAWS, both of which share a browse/focus interaction model and Windows-specific keyboard commands. Nothing in this matrix would catch the reflow failure from this domain's magnification lesson, the aria-activedescendant gap from the keyboard lesson, or the aria-label mismatch from the voice-control lesson — an entire category of finding per unused access method, invisible by construction, no matter how many Windows/screen-reader pairings get added.
feedback.too-many-browsers: Testing across browsers isn't wasteful in principle — different browsers do genuinely expose different accessibility-tree bugs, especially around ARIA support gaps. The actual critique isn't "too many browsers," it's that every added row here is still testing the same underlying interaction model, so the marginal value of a fourth Windows/screen-reader row is much lower than the marginal value of the very first non-screen-reader row this matrix doesn't have at all.
feedback.jaws-unnecessary: JAWS remains heavily used, particularly in enterprise and government contexts — dropping it isn't the fix, and it isn't even the actual problem with this proposal. The problem is that adding JAWS to an all-Windows, all-screen-reader matrix doesn't diversify anything that matters; JAWS and NVDA are different products but the same category of test.

contentSections.mechanism: A test matrix's value comes from the union of bug categories its rows can each independently catch, not from the row count. Four rows that all share one interaction model and one OS test one category of failure four times over; two rows that each represent a genuinely different access method — a screen reader and a magnification pass, say — test two categories once each, and that second matrix will surface more distinct real-world defects on a typical page despite having half the rows.

contentSections.scenario: You're deciding what belongs on Havenmark's AT test matrix for the checkout flow specifically — the highest-risk path on the site.
contentSections.question: Select every row that earns a place in a P0 (must-test) matrix for checkout, based on genuinely distinct coverage.

items.label: NVDA + Firefox, Windows
VoiceOver + Safari, macOS
VoiceOver + Safari, iOS
Keyboard-only pass, no screen reader, Chrome/Windows
400% browser zoom / reflow pass, any modern browser
Voice Control pass, macOS
NVDA + Chrome, Windows (in addition to NVDA + Firefox)
JAWS + Chrome, Windows
Narrator + Edge, Windows

explanation.nvda-firefox-windows: P0. The single most common desktop screen reader combination by usage survey data, and the default reference pairing NVDA's own documentation is written against.
explanation.voiceover-safari-macos: P0. A genuinely distinct interaction model from NVDA, and Safari/VoiceOver has historically been where ARIA support gaps between browsers show up first.
explanation.voiceover-safari-ios: P0. Not optional for any site with real mobile traffic — VoiceOver is the only screen reader on iOS, so this is the entire blind-iPhone-user population's experience of checkout, tested or not.
explanation.keyboard-only-chrome: P0. Catches an entire category — focus order, focus visibility, traps, aria-activedescendant wiring — that no screen reader pass reliably surfaces on its own, since a screen reader user navigating by heading or landmark commands may never traverse the page in strict Tab order the way this pass specifically checks.
explanation.zoom-400-reflow: P0. Checkout is the highest-value page on the site for a low-vision user who never touches a screen reader at all; reflow failures are invisible to every other row on this list.
explanation.voice-control-macos: P0 for a revenue-critical path specifically because of WCAG 2.5.3's operational bite — a single mismatched aria-label can make a form genuinely uncompletable by voice, which is a full task-failure, not a degraded experience.
explanation.nvda-chrome-second-browser: Not P0. This shares NVDA's entire interaction model with the row already included; the marginal finding rate on a second browser engine, while non-zero, is real P1 spot-check territory rather than must-test, given the budget already committed to five genuinely distinct rows above.
explanation.jaws-chrome-windows: Not P0 for a mid-size EU retail checkout specifically — JAWS remains important, especially for engagements with known enterprise or government users, but for this site's actual traffic profile it's reasonable P1 coverage rather than a row that has to happen before sign-off, given NVDA already covers the same interaction model on the P0 list.
explanation.narrator-edge-windows: Not P0. Narrator has real but comparatively small usage share per the same survey data this matrix is grounded in, and shares Windows's keyboard conventions with the NVDA row already present — a reasonable P2 (documented, not actively tested this cycle) rather than a budget-consuming P0 row.

contentSections.synthesis: Six P0 rows, five access methods, three operating systems, zero redundant interaction models — that's what "defensible" means here. Every excluded combination has a stated reason tied to either usage data or model overlap with something already included, not "we ran out of time and stopped alphabetically." A client reading this matrix should be able to disagree with a specific row's tier and say why, which is the actual point of writing the reasoning down rather than just delivering a list.

contentSections.body:
**The artefact itself: a brief, a rubric, and a worked exemplar.**

**The brief**, as it would actually arrive from Havenmark: *"Before remediation sign-off, we need to know which AT and browser combinations were tested on checkout and account management, and your reasoning for anything you didn't test. Legal needs to reference this matrix if a complaint under the EAA cites a specific assistive technology we didn't cover."*

**The rubric** a reviewer — internal lead, or the client's own accessibility contact — would grade this against:
- *Coverage of access-method categories*: does the P0 tier include at least one row from each of screen reader, keyboard-only, magnification/reflow, and voice or switch, rather than clustering in one category?
- *Mobile representation*: is there at least one mobile combination (VoiceOver+iOS or TalkBack+Android) on a site with real mobile traffic, not just desktop rows?
- *Grounded reasoning, not vibes*: does every row's inclusion or exclusion cite something concrete — usage data, interaction-model difference, or this specific site's risk profile — rather than "industry standard" asserted without support?
- *Explicit tiering*: are rows sorted into P0 (must-test, blocks sign-off), P1 (spot-checked or tested on a sample of pages, not the full flow), and P2 (documented as a known gap, not tested this cycle) — rather than one undifferentiated list?
- *Actionable exclusions*: for anything left out entirely, is there a stated reason a client could push back on, rather than silence?

**A worked exemplar row**, showing the level of specificity the matrix needs — not a template to fill in, a real filled-in example:

| AT / Input | Browser / OS | Scope | Tier | Why |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| VoiceOver | Safari / iOS 17 | Checkout, full flow | P0 | Only screen reader on iOS; site has 38% mobile checkout starts per analytics; distinct interaction model (Rotor, no browse/focus split) from every desktop row |
| Keyboard only | Chrome / Windows | Checkout + account, full flow | P0 | Catches focus-order, trap, and activedescendant defects invisible to landmark/heading-based screen reader navigation |
| 400% browser zoom | Chrome, any OS | Checkout, full flow | P0 | Reflow failures affect low-vision users independent of screen reader use; checkout is highest-value page for this population |
| JAWS | Chrome / Windows | Checkout, smoke test only | P1 | Same interaction model as NVDA (already P0); spot-checked for JAWS-specific rendering differences, not full-flow tested, given budget already committed above |
| TalkBack | Chrome / Android | Product listing only | P2 | Mobile traffic skews heavily iOS for this client per analytics; documented gap, revisit if Android share changes materially |

An AT test matrix isn't a coverage report — it's an argument. Every included row should defend itself with usage data, a genuinely distinct interaction model, or this specific site's risk profile; every excluded combination should have a stated reason a client could disagree with. That's the difference between "we tested accessibility" and a document someone can actually act on when a complaint names a specific tool you did or didn't cover.
